alt: The isnad is drawn as a chain: A told me that B said that C heard the Prophet (pbuh) say. Below it the matn, the text itself, reports what the Prophet said, did or approved. A note defines the Sunnah as his way of life, known mainly through Hadiths.
caption: Isnad is the chain of narrators; matn is the text they passed on.

alt: Four stages in order: memorising and some note-taking in the Prophet's lifetime; teaching by companions and successors with early sahifas; the order of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (ruled 717–720) to collect Hadiths in writing; and the musannaf and musnad collections of the second and third Islamic centuries, followed by the six Sunni collections.
caption: From memory to notebooks to official collection to the great compilations.

alt: Side-by-side comparison. A musannaf groups Hadiths by subject, such as prayer, fasting or trade (al-Muwatta of Imam Malik, the Musannaf of Abd al-Razzaq). A musnad groups them by the companion who narrated them (the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal).
caption: Musannaf: by subject. Musnad: by narrator.

after: ## How did scholars test whether a Hadith was reliable?
alt: Two checklists feed one grade. Isnad criticism checks narrators' character, memory, whether they could have met and that there is no gap in the chain. Matn criticism checks the text against the Qur'an, established Hadiths, reason and the Prophet's character. Results are sahih (sound), hasan (good), da'if (weak), or fabricated and rejected.
caption: Both the chain and the text are tested before a Hadith is graded.

after: ## What are the four Shi'a collections?
alt: Three compilers and their four books: al-Kulayni compiled al-Kafi, covering belief as well as law; Ibn Babawayh (al-Shaykh al-Saduq) compiled Man la yahduruhu al-faqih; al-Shaykh al-Tusi compiled Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar. The last three focus mainly on law.
caption: Three compilers, four books; only al-Kafi covers belief as well as law.

after: ## How are the Hadiths used in Islamic law?
alt: Four stepped levels: the Qur'an as the first source; Hadiths and the Sunnah second, explaining, detailing and filling gaps; ijma', the consensus of scholars; and qiyas, analogy, illustrated by extending the ban on wine to other intoxicants.
caption: Hadiths are the second source of law, after the Qur'an and before ijma' and qiyas.
